industrySeats.why: The hoard-guarding dragon of the Vǫlsunga cycle — Wagner's Ring and Tolkien's Smaug both descend from him; every treasure-vault boss in the genre is his descendant.
The cursed hoard of Andvari is greed made plot — the gold that buys kingdoms and kills its owners; finance's oldest cautionary tale wears his coils.
Wagner casts him as the giant-turned-dragon of Siegfried; the greatest cycle in opera is partly his story.
The Vǫlsunga saga and the Nibelungenlied are the heroic literature of the North — and he is their dragon.
The dragon-slayer of the Vǫlsunga cycle — the hero-versus-dragon encounter as a standing character archetype across games and anime.
The Vǫlsunga saga and the Nibelungenlied made him the North's great hero; the dragon-slayer plot is his patent.
Wagner's Siegfried is the hero of the Ring cycle — two of opera's four great nights carry his story.
The weapon that defends Ásgarðr and Miðgarðr from the giants — the shield-wall of the worlds in a single hammer.
The Þórr's-hammer amulet is the most-worn pendant of the Viking Age; archaeology recovers it by the thousand and jewelers cast it still.
The most famous weapon in modern mythic IP — Marvel's Mjolnir and God of War made the hammer a franchise logo.
Forged by the dwarfs Sindri and Brokkr — the masterwork of divine smithcraft, short handle and all.
The rainbow bridge is the portal level of every Norse game, and the MCU's Bifröst made it franchise iconography.
The rainbow made architecture — the visible spectrum as a road between worlds; optics' oldest image.
The bridge that spans Miðgarðr and Ásgarðr — joining two worlds is the industry's founding dream, guarded and load-bearing.
The link between two worlds, watched by Heimdallr — the connection itself, with a sentry on the endpoint.
The moon personified, driving its chariot across the night sky — the Norse moon made god, pursued nightly by Hati.
The night watch himself; the moon that governs every sleeping hour is his face.
Moon and month share his name's root in every Germanic language; the first calendar counted by his phases.
The ski-borne huntress of the winter mountains — Þrymheimr's snowfields are her domain; the outdoor industry is her cult.
The skalds call her ǫndurdís — the ski-lady; winter sports' patron deity, bow in hand.
Norway's ski resorts and winter peaks trade on her legend; the failed mountain honeymoon of Njǫrðr's marriage is tourism's oldest complaint.

curatedPairs.note: The Vǫlsunga core: Sigurðr slays Fáfnir on Reginn's counsel and takes the cursed hoard — slayer and dragon bound in one cycle.
The dragon-slayer and the valkyrie — betrothed on the mountain, betrayed by the ale of forgetfulness, united only in death.

curatedPairs.relationship: The Vǫlsunga cycle: brothers divided by the hoard
curatedPairs.note: Reginn the smith plots, Fáfnir the dragon guards — the cursed gold of Andvari sets brother against brother and kills them both.

curatedPairs.relationship: The Vǫlsunga cycle: foster-father and foster-son
curatedPairs.note: Reginn reforges Gram and sends Sigurðr against his own brother — then plots the hero's murder and dies by the same blade.
Greek and Norse strong-heroes who win imperishable glory by killing monsters — the labors and the dragon-fight as the same plot.
The two great serpents of Norse tradition — the hoard-dragon of the Vǫlsunga cycle and the world-serpent of Ragnarök.
Norse and Greek personifications of the moon itself — not merely lunar deities but the moon made god and goddess.
Norse and Japanese male moon deities — the rarer masculine face of the moon across world pantheons.
Norse and Greek rainbows as the passage between gods and mortals — the bridge that is walked and the messenger who walks it.
Heimdallr keeps his watch at Himinbjǫrg where the rainbow bridge meets heaven — the sentry and the span are one institution.
Sindri and Brokkr's masterworks, won in the same wager with Loki's head as the stake — the hammer and the self-multiplying ring.
